title: High School Science Profile Predicts Adults’ Views on the Future of AI and STS
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether high school science experiences are associated with later adult use of artificial intelligence (AI) and with adults’ views about AI and science–technology–society (STS) issues. The motivation is a broader question in science education: whether K-12 science learning has long-term effects on how people engage with AI in adulthood.

The study does not test an AI-powered instructional tool or compare AI versus non-AI conditions. Instead, it uses longitudinal panel data from the Korea Employment Education Panel (KEEP) II, following a cohort of Korean general high school students from 2016 to 2023. The analytic sample included 2,348 participants. High school science interest and science achievement were measured during secondary school, and adult AI use, AI perceptions, and STS views were measured at age 24.

Using structural equation modeling, the author found that science achievement in high school positively predicted later AI use, whereas science interest did not directly predict AI use. Adult AI use was associated with both positive and negative perceptions of AI, and these perceptions in turn related to views on human–AI relations, future quality of life, and the concentration of benefits from science and technology. The main conclusion is that stronger high school science achievement is linked to later AI engagement and AI-related attitudes, but the paper is correlational and does not provide causal evidence about an educational AI intervention.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed longitudinal correlational study using panel SEM, not a causal comparison of AI-powered tools versus non-AI comparators in K-12 science learning. It does not meet RCT/QED standards for intervention evidence and is adjacent to the requested topic rather than directly within it.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no instructional intervention effect on K-12 science reasoning or inquiry outcomes. Its findings concern long-term associations between high school science achievement and later adult AI use/perceptions, so it does not provide direct evidence of impact for the target domain.
